title: Nginx and HTTPS
summary: Forward public requests to a private Spring Boot process, then configure HTTPS.

sources.title: Spring Boot: traditional deployment and proxy configuration

richText: Use Nginx as a reverse proxy
A reverse proxy receives a client request and forwards it to another server.
Nginx can accept public requests and forward them to the Spring Boot process on the same VPS.
Bind Spring Boot to 127.0.0.1 so its HTTP port accepts only local connections.
Expose the public web ports through Nginx.

example.title: Forward HTTP requests to the local application
description: The Spring Boot process listens at 127.0.0.1:8080.
Use a domain you control in server_name. This example uses journal.example.com.
Place this server block in the Nginx configuration location used by your Linux distribution.
This is the HTTP proxy step. Add the HTTPS configuration described below before exposing authenticated application traffic.
explanation: proxy_pass selects the local application server.
Host preserves the requested domain. X-Forwarded-Proto identifies the original request protocol.
Only trust forwarded headers from the controlled proxy. Restrict direct access to the application.
If Spring must use forwarded headers for redirects, configure its forwarded-header handling for this proxy arrangement.
Validate the Nginx configuration before reloading it.
example.commands:
sudo nginx -t
sudo systemctl reload nginx

richText: Point the domain’s DNS record to the VPS.
Install a TLS certificate for that domain and configure Nginx to serve HTTPS on port 443.
TLS encrypts traffic between the browser and the public server.
Redirect public HTTP traffic to HTTPS once HTTPS works.
Keep automatic certificate renewal configured and check that renewed certificates are loaded.
Forward the public HTTPS protocol correctly so generated URLs and OAuth callback URLs use HTTPS.
Allow required SSH and public web ports. Keep the application port private.
Preserve working SSH access when changing remote firewall rules.
Choose proxy timeouts and request-size limits for the application’s endpoints.
Rate limiting can reduce repeated abusive requests. It does not prevent every denial-of-service attack.
Check the local application, public HTTPS endpoint and certificate independently.
Then check an authenticated operation that reads or writes the database.
